_comment: Pages read on 2026-10-24 for the true-credits batch: one record per citation added. passage and note: the passage id and the 0-based index of the note in its layers list in config/layers.json; kind: the note's kind; source and on: the citation as config/layers.json gives it; url: the page the citation links to, read on the date and at the UTC time given. These pages were read with a text reader that returns the page's text but no HTTP status, final URL or SHA-256, so the records give none; time is the UTC time taken right after the read.

status: "added" (cited from this batch; read_for says why). quote: the writer's words as found on the page, only for public-domain writers; spelling, misprints and abbreviations are the page's own. pointer: for the Pulpit Commentary (Bible Hub's text carries BibleSoft's copyright notice), where on the page the point is made, never its words.

verdict (founder's decision 20): whether the cited comment respects or denies Scripture, judged on its own words. decided: for a chapter 1 page, what its introduction says on who wrote the book (decision 23(3)).

left_out: the readings behind the cites removed on this date. denies: the page behind each entry added to denies in config/layer-sources.json on this date, with the cites it removed (passages moved to docs/held are listed there instead); not_stating: a cite read again that does not state its note's point (removed, or kept with counts: false for what else it supports); held: the passages set aside; held_reads: each page read on this date in looking for a second writer for a held passage, one record per source, verse and note (Bullinger has two on Ecclesiastes 3:18, the Companion Bible and Figures of Speech; note is the index in the passage as docs/held/layers-2026-10-24.json keeps it). writer: the cite list's writer for that book (unnamed when the part names none); states: whether he states the note's point in his own words; quote: his words, for public-domain writers, where he states it or comes nearest; pointer: for the Pulpit Commentary, where on the page; finding: what he says on the point.

held_reads.finding: Bullock gives a literal rendering ending "that they are beasts, they themselves" and a note on the Septuagint and Syriac reading showing for seeing, but he never says the pronoun is doubled or that the doubling is a figure of emphasis, so his rendering alone does not state the point.
He says men have made themselves beasts by brutish ways; no Hebrew and nothing on the pronoun.

The Companion Bible's notes on this verse gloss God might manifest them as God having chosen to show them that even they are beasts and define beasts as living creatures, but name no figure (its only Epizeuxis note in the chapter is on iniquity in verse 16) and do not say the Hebrew says they twice.
He quotes another author's translation and applies it to corrupt magistrates; no remark on the repeated pronoun.
The Geneva notes give only note (h) on this verse, "And made them pure in their first creation", and say nothing about the Hebrew saying they twice.
He says men see they are beasts through the fall and gives Broughton's rendering, but says nothing of the doubled pronoun or its emphasis (read again at 13:12:50Z).
He treats 3:16 to 22 together as humbling proud men; nothing on the Hebrew wording.
He says God proves men so they see their mortal frailty like the beasts; nothing on the pronoun.
He notes the Hebrew reads that they are beasts to themselves and gives two senses; nothing on the repetition or its emphasis (read again at 13:12:58Z).

Wesley says God suffers these disorders so that he might discover men to themselves, who by their brutish practices have made themselves like beasts; he says nothing about the Hebrew saying they twice or about emphasis.
Bullock explains that the long delay of God's judgment shows people that their short lives leave them unable to follow His justice, and says nothing about hemmah echoing the sound of behemah.
No Hebrew for this verse.
The Companion Bible's notes on this verse (God, God might manifest them, beasts) mark no play on words and do not mention hemmah echoing behemah.

A search of Figures of Speech finds Ecclesiastes 3:18 only under Epizeuxis (scan page 248) and Pleonasm (scan page 462), and the word behemah does not occur, so he does not state the sound echo. Read through archive.org's full-text search of the same scan.
He does not mention behemah or hemmah; his only Hebrew in this section is ruach, on verse 21.
The Geneva notes on this verse (note h, on God making man pure at creation) do not mention the Hebrew words or any echo of behemah in hemmah.
No Hebrew in his note and no play on words or likeness of sound.
No discussion of the Hebrew words.
No Hebrew play on beasts or they.
Only a gloss that the Hebrew reads beasts to themselves; no play on words.
Wesley's note on this verse is about God showing people their own state and does not mention the sound of hemmah echoing behemah or any play on words.

Jamieson reads the return to the ground as the point where man became mortal and cites only Romans 5:12 and 1 Timothy 2:15, with no reference to Ecclesiastes.

held_reads.quote: Formed out of the dust, he shall return to dust again.
held_reads.finding: Keil explains that man, formed from dust, returns to dust, and cites Genesis, Isaiah, Job, Psalm 104 and Romans 8 on verses 17 to 19, but not Ecclesiastes.

held_reads.quote: thou shalt return unto dust in thy body, whilst the immortal spirit shall return unto God who gave it, Ecclesiastes 12:7.
held_reads.finding: Poole points Genesis 3:19 to Ecclesiastes 12:7 (and 1:13 on toil) but not to Ecclesiastes 3:20.

held_reads.quote: Unto dust shalt thou return - Thy body shall be forsaken by thy soul, and become itself a lump of dust,
held_reads.finding: Wesley's note (the same words Benson later used) describes the body becoming dust in the grave and cites no Bible reference, so it does not point to Ecclesiastes 3:20.
Plumptre renders desolation as tempest and makes the storm a type of the suddenness of God's judgment, and says nothing about the Hebrew words for distress and anguish.

Benson covers the verse in his note on 1:24 to 28, taking desolation as a sudden judgment over a whole country and the whirlwind as swift ruin, and says nothing about the Hebrew words for distress and anguish.

Bullinger glosses desolation as tempest and destruction as calamity, and his note on verse 26 marks an Introversion (a reversed order of fear, desolation, destruction and anguish across verses 26 and 27), which is a word-order figure, not a sound-play; the www form of the link in the cite list failed to load three times, so the page was read at this address without www.
Clarke's only note on the verse is on the whirlwind (kesuphah), where he says sense and sound are well expressed in that one word; he says nothing on distress and anguish or on their sounding alike.
Ellicott's volume has no note on verse 27 (its notes go from verse 26 to 28, and Bible Hub's verse page shows no Ellicott text for 1:27), so J. W. Nutt says nothing on the point.
The Geneva note on the verse only explains fear as the destruction they feared, and says nothing about distress and anguish or their sound.
Gill reads the verse as foretelling the Roman ruin of Jerusalem and Judea, with distress and anguish as the sword and famine of the siege, and says nothing about the two Hebrew words sounding alike.

Matthew Henry says the sinners' fright will turn to despair as distress and anguish come on them like a deluge and a whirlwind, with cross references on anguish, but says nothing about the Hebrew words sounding alike.
The Concise Commentary treats the verse only within its note on 1:20 to 33, saying sinners' calamity will come, and does not mention distress and anguish or any sound-play.
Fausset glosses each word (distress with cross references to Psalm 4:1 and 44:11, anguish as inextricable oppression and deepest despair) but never mentions the Hebrew words or their sound.

held_reads.quote: The alliterating words צרה וצוּקה, cf. Isaiah 30:6; Zephaniah 1:15,
held_reads.finding: Delitzsch states the sound-play, calling the two words alliterating and saying Proverbs is fond of such rhymes, but his Proverbs 1 comments are left out by denies in config/layer-sources.json, so he cannot be cited; this was read on Bible Hub's 1:27 verse page while checking the Ellicott gap, not on his chapter page.
Poole comments only on desolation (a desolating sword or judgment) and the whirlwind, and says nothing about the Hebrew words for distress and anguish.

held_reads.pointer: In the Exposition note on verse 27, in the part on distress and anguish that follows the remark on the whirlwind and comes before the closing remark on a clause the Septuagint adds: it names the Hebrew pair, says they alliterate, points to Isaiah 30:6 and Zephaniah 1:15, and explains the roots of both words.
held_reads.finding: The Pulpit Commentary's exposition on 1:27 states that the Hebrew words for distress and anguish alliterate, comparing Isaiah 30:6 and Zephaniah 1:15, and explains what each word's root means.
Wesley has no note on verse 27 (his notes on the chapter skip from verse 26 to 28), so he says nothing on the point.
